Exclusive: Report says restricting cars and freeing up pavement space could be a cheap way to entice shoppers

The long decline of the high street is a problem that has gripped British governments for years. But what if there was a solution no one had considered before – doing it all on the cheap?

Spending less money is, admittedly, just one element of a report led by the urban thinktank Create Streets. But it does argue that rather than multimillion-pound revamps, a better answer could be smaller changes aimed at making town and city centres more appealing.

Central to this, the study says, is trying to banish, or at least tame, motor traffic, because too often urban centres are places “designed to be driven through, not for time to be spent in”.

As well as citing a lack of imagination, the report blames planning regulations that favour conformity and clutter and too often treat speeding cars as a given, to which everything else must adjust.

“The default high street is engineered for traffic and furnished from a catalogue: a tarmac pavement, guardrails penning people at the kerb, litter bins ordered from a procurement catalogue, a row of plastic planters – public investment that is joyless,” it says.

While planners have traditionally focused on car access as a metric for thriving town centres, calculations for the Create Streets report suggest that replacing parking with other kerbside infrastructure, including bike spaces or outside drinking and dining areas, creates more economic value.

It found that one parking space in the high street of a market town is typically used by about 3.5 vehicles a day, bringing in just over £73,000 a year in spending to nearby shops.

But the same 12 square metres, if used to hold nine share e-bikes, generates an average of 13 trips a day, with over £146,000 a year in spending, even taking into account the lower average spend per person.

In a busier city, where share bikes would be used more frequently, the estimated total annual spend rises to more than £300,000.

Repurposing the space for outside dining brings less dramatic gains, but in a city centre it can still amount to about £120,000 in extra annual spending.

The report, also produced by Cyclehoop, which makes bike storage, calls for a cultural rethink involving low-cost tweaks that rip away ugly and unnecessary street furniture and make better use of kerbsides.

Calling use by families “the indicator species of a healthy high street”, the report cites what is known as “the wrist test” – whether it feels safe to let go of a young child’s wrist so they can roam with some freedom.

This is best done, it argues, by removing the threat of speeding motor vehicles and not by trying to mitigate their impact. It calls the removal of pedestrian guardrails next to roads “the most cost-effective upgrade for the majority of high streets”, saying they are an eyesore with minimal safety benefits.

The report says “the absurdity of modern public realm management” is exemplified by Secured by Design, policy guidelines on cutting neighbourhood crime. These can, critics point out, mean benches and plants are removed on the advice of police, supposedly to discourage antisocial behaviour.

Andy Burnham, the prime minister, has pledged to try to reverse the decline of high streets, announcing in September a £210m regeneration fund.

However, the bulk of the money will go into buildings: turning old shops into shared workspaces or community cafes, or keeping pubs and clubs in business.

The report argues that renovating buildings is pointless if the street outside is unappealing. To reduce clutter, it says, there should be “a presumption of removal where an item cannot be justified”.

The effects can be dramatic, the report says, pointing to examples including Altrincham in Cheshire, where the creation of a walkable, car-free urban area helped see retail vacancies fall from over 30% to 7% in less than a decade.

Such initiatives do not have to be expensive, it claims, noting the example of an unused patch of land next to a church in Grimsby which was turned into a park for less than £20,000.

“Streets that are ugly are not so because councils lack the desire to change them, but because the system is counting the maintenance liabilities, not the benefits,” said David Milner of Create Streets.

“What works is cheap: trees in the ground, benches people want to sit on, clutter taken away.

“So much of what is built now seems to be temporary, looking more like road works than public realm improvements, so we encourage the concept of permanence; more trees in the ground, not in giant plant pots, for example.”

A spokesperson for the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government said: “We support local leaders to make decisions on pedestrianisation based on their communities’ needs.

“Our Hope on the High Street strategy will help local people revive town centres by protecting community assets, bringing derelict buildings back into use and tackling the spread of vape and gambling shops.

“Funding is available for local leaders to spend on their priorities, including pedestrianising and regenerating their high streets if they so wish.”

items.lbText:
President purchased up to $5m of stock before revoking Biden-era rule that limited Nvidia’s ability to sell to China

Donald Trump bought Nvidia stock worth millions of dollars as he made decisions on America’s China policy that would benefit the chipmaker, an analysis has found .

In May 2025, Trump’s administration rescinded a Biden-era rule designed to prevent the most advanced US-made AI chips from being exported to China.

This rule aimed to strengthen the US’s own chip industry and to protect America from what was widely regarded as a national security threat: the possibility that China might develop superior AI.

In the days before he rescinded the rule, Trump’s public financial disclosures indicate that he bought between $1m (£760,000) and $5m worth of Nvidia stock – a purchase noted in an analysis by the anti-corruption group DeKleptocracy.

He also bought shares in other tech companies, including Apple, Meta and Microsoft.

The diffusion rule would have limited Nvidia’s ability to sell to what has been one of its largest markets: China accounted for about a quarter of the company’s sales between 2010 and 2022. Nvidia’s shares rose in value just after Trump announced the rescission of the rule, and after he had bought the stock.

In December 2025 Trump said he would allow Nvidia to sell H200 chips to China, a decision that was greenlit by the Department of Commerce in January 2026. This was a controversial move. H200s were one of the company’s most advanced chips – six times better than what was available in China at the time, said experts.

The Council on Foreign Relations suggested selling H200s would “supercharge” China’s future AI factories and strengthen the US’s rival.

Trump’s public financial disclosures indicate he made at least three purchases of Nvidia shares in the days after announcing this, all of them between $250,001 and $500,000.

These trades are among Trump’s larger purchases of Nvidia stock, although he appears to have made dozens of transactions involving the chipmaker’s shares since taking office.

DeKleptocracy wrote in its analysis: “While the country debates how a possible Chinese spy may have manipulated White House policy for one AI company, it must grapple with how Trump’s corruption may have motivated him to deliver the entire AI industry’s technology to China.”

The US – and the global economy – have been grappling with revelations that Jensen Huang , Nvidia’s former chief executive, had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang.

Reports have suggested this relationship allowed Alice Huang’s company, Megaspeed, to obtain billions of dollars worth of Nvidia’s chips, even as other companies struggled.

Trump was twice briefed by US intelligence officials on their conclusions that Alice Huang was a Chinese asset. He did not act on this assessment.

Jensen Huang has been described as a close Trump ally and has met the president a number of times. Nvidia made a $25m contribution to Trump’s ballroom in October 2025, with Huang saying he was “delighted to be a part of it”.

items.lbText:
Hannah Walker says systems designed to minimise expenditure in the name of efficiency can end up less capable of fulfilling their actual purpose

The article by Steven Strogatz and Alex Townsend on the dangers of excessive optimisation identifies a problem extending far beyond mathematics and artificial intelligence ( The efficiency trap: why optimising everything can backfire, badly, 8 November ).

The widespread adoption of just-in-time supply chains illustrates it perfectly. By eliminating inventories and spare capacity, businesses reduced costs and improved efficiency, but frequently transferred those savings into risks that remained invisible until something went wrong. The disruption of global manufacturing during the pandemic exposed the consequences.

The same thinking has shaped public services and national defence. Hospital beds, experienced staff, strategic stockpiles and redundant infrastructure can all appear wasteful when measured against immediate demand. Yet their value lies precisely in their availability when circumstances cease to be normal.

Europe’s dependence on American military capabilities provides a particularly troubling example. What appeared financially efficient in peacetime has created strategic vulnerabilities as the reliability of US commitments comes into question.

The fundamental error is not optimisation itself, but optimising the wrong objective. A system designed to minimise expenditure may succeed brilliantly at doing so while becoming progressively less capable of fulfilling its actual purpose. Resilience is not inefficiency. It is a form of insurance. Like all insurance, the value only becomes apparent when it is needed – usually in a crisis. Hannah Walker Wymondham, Leicestershire

items.title: Fight the climate crisis or go for growth? There is a way Burnham can do both | Jonathan Freedland
items.author: Jonathan Freedland
items.content:
The environmental and economic dilemmas he faces are formidable but, with a bold plan, he could set an example for leaders around the world

For politicians of the centre-left especially, it’s the great dilemma of the age. How do you do what everyone can see is essential to save the planet from boiling – even as your voters demand action to get the economy growing and to make life more affordable? Plenty of activists will tell you there’s no contradiction, that tackling the climate crisis makes economic as well as ecological sense and, in the long term, you know they’re right. But you don’t live in the long term. You’re running the government right now and facing several unavoidable, binary choices.

Andy Burnham is a prime example. This week, he addressed the Cop summit in Antalya, promising “a new era of British leadership” in the struggle against global heating. It’s important to him to talk that way: his political strategy relies on shrinking the appeal of the Green party, whose electoral success earlier this year helped remove his predecessor. But talk only takes you so far. Eventually the words have to be matched by action.

Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

items.lbText:
JLR chief executive calls for EU and Britain to join forces amid competition from Chinese electric carmakers

Jaguar Land Rover has reported a £451m quarterly loss as it counts the cost of cutting 4,000 jobs, while its chief executive has called for the EU and Britain to work together in the face of competition from China.

Britain’s largest automotive employer reported revenues rising to £5.9bn between July and September, but it recorded £530m in costs from the job cuts announced near the end of that period amid tough trading conditions.

JLR said it expected the vast majority of the job cuts to be achieved via voluntary redundancies, with 3,000 already confirmed. Most of those people will leave at the end of November.

JLR said it had scraped into profit from its operations if it ignored the restructuring costs, but it was hurt by falling sales in China and the Middle East.

Many European carmakers are struggling as they face competition from Chinese rivals at the same time as they invest in electric car production.

PB Balaji, JLR’s chief executive, said on Friday the “onslaught of competition” from China meant the UK and EU should stop plans for new post-Brexit trade barriers on each other.

The automotive industry is lobbying the UK and EU intensely to delay the implementation of “rules of origin” on 1 January, which threaten to impose 10% tariffs on UK-EU electric cars that use batteries from Asia. The EU is also considering “made in Europe” rules that would lock UK-made cars out of subsidies.

“Now is the time for actually fostering this entire electrical ecosystem,” Balaji said. “It’s so important for us that we all hold hands, stick together and ensure that we get the system to evolve into the world of electrics.”

He added: “We just need time to ensure all these plans start coming into fruition.”

The company, which is owned by the Indian conglomerate Tata, previously sought to target China for growth, only to write off billions in investments in 2019 as a new wave of Chinese carmakers led to massive overcapacity in the country.

JLR, which was last year hit by a devastating hack , is targeting growth in the US, where it is in the process of agreeing a deal for the Chrysler owner, Stellantis, to manufacture Land Rovers for the first time.

JLR has started to produce electric Land Rovers, beginning with its flagship Range Rover, built in Solihull in the West Midlands. Electric versions of its cheaper, higher-selling Range Rover Sport, Defender and Defender Sport will follow.

It also produces the luxury electric Jaguar Type 01, and Balaji said JLR was working on a new version of the Discovery.

items.lbText:
From Calvin Klein to British Vogue, the Real Madrid man is leading the way when it comes to football’s foray into fashion. But is he playing it safe?

T his Sunday, Jude Bellingham will line up with his England teammates for a match against Spain. But the footballer has been hitting the headlines way beyond the pitch recently – thanks to fronting a Calvin Klein underwear ad released this month, and becoming the first footballer to appear solo on the cover of British Vogue .

It’s a savvy move for the 23-year-old, future-proofing himself as a power player both on and off the pitch. This is a roadmap carved out by David Beckham, who since retiring in 2013 has become a brand and personality that transcends sport. Beckham – together with his wife, Victoria – became a billionaire this year.

The Calvin Klein ads, which feature Bellingham in underwear, sometimes in his signature Christ the Redeemer pose, have caused a stir since appearing in London and New York, with passersby stopping to take selfies. The popularity of a billboard in Soho, New York also cements his celebrity status in the US after this summer’s World Cup.

Of course Bellingham is a bona fide star on the pitch. Mark Borkowski, a public relations consultant, says this factor is pivotal to the footballer’s crossover appeal. “Bellingham is an exceptional sporting talent, and his brand value is understandably enormous,” he says. “But fashion doesn’t create that value, football does. Fashion merely provides another means of exploiting it.”

This buzz is working out well for Calvin Klein. The fashion data firm Launchmetrics said in 48 hours the Calvin Klein campaign generated $35.8m (£27m) in media impact value, the metric that works out the monetary value of social media posts. The fashion platform Lyst reports that searches for Calvin Klein underwear have risen by 25% since the campaign was released.

Bellingham has a savvy team around him, with his mother, Denise, a former HR executive, working as his personal manager. Some are wondering if his 21-year-old brother, Jobe – in the England squad for the first time this month – might do similar campaigns, increasing the rise of the Bellingham brand.

So far Bellingham – and his management team – have been strategic with his brand choices. As well as Calvin Klein, Bellingham works with Adidas, Kim Kardashian’s underwear brand Skims and Louis Vuitton.

Daniel-Yaw Miller, in his influential SportsVerse newsletter , compared him to Beckham. “It’s very intentional,” he says. “What [Bellingham is] doing is aimed at the higher tier of the market but at the same time, a big part of his personality is very relatable.”

Bellingham is also a heart-throb, with looks that, in another life, could belong to a boyband. Vogue have amped up this factor: the magazine comes with a pull-out poster. “It helps that he’s incredibly good-looking,” says Miller.

Bellingham is not the only male footballer to work with the fashion industry. Bukayo Saka and Son Heung-min were in Burberry’s autumn campaign, Kylian Mbappé worked with Christian Dior, and Declan Rice is on the cover of GQ this month. “The earnings that they can get during their football career are obviously huge,” says Miller. “But what sets them up for life beyond that is being brands and businesses in their own right. It’s not only just a money thing. It’s about cementing a legacy and securing their profile in the game long term, commercially and culturally.”

Not everyone is impressed by Bellingham’s foray into fashion. Felicia Pennant, the editor of the football and fashion magazine Season, says if he is following Beckham’s business model, the older footballer pushed the boundaries more, appearing in edgy photoshoots covered in (fake) blood for The Face magazine in 2001, and in artwork by Sam Taylor-Johnson . “Beckham was the subject of art and he was the art rather than selling the art,” she says. “I think what Jude’s doing feels quite transactional … there’s nothing that directional about anything he’s done so far.”

Borkowski sounds a note of caution going forward. “Fame surrounds exceptional young athletes with people whose livelihoods depend on telling them how wonderful they are. That can become a very dangerous echo chamber,” he says. “The football makes the myth. The business can preserve it. But hubris can destroy both.”

items.lbText:
Signing of agreement to smooth movement of food, plants and animals next week will not recoup huge sums firms were forced to spend

The removal of border checks and paperwork on plant imports will “dissolve” £60m of annual costs for the horticulture industry when the UK and EU’s new post-Brexit deal comes in, the environment secretary has said.

Before the UK-EU summit on 20 November , Angela Eagle said she hoped paperwork headaches for importers would “disappear” after the changes, although the move would not help businesses recoup the large sums they spent to deal with border controls.

“If we get the ink dry on 20 November, which I very much hope we will … all of that uncertainty, the extra cost, the paperwork and the potential problems if things get stuck at borders would all disappear,” Eagle told the Guardian during a visit to a plant nursery in Kent.

“The cost, that £60m, can just dissolve and people’s potential to both export back into the EU and get their imports in … gets easier and more predictable.”

The UK’s departure from the bloc triggered the introduction of border checks on imports and exports of plants, food and animal products, from sausages and cheese to trees and leather goods.

Exports of British food and drink to the EU have collapsed by more than a third since Brexit, according to analysis by the National Farmers’ Union, with egg, chicken and potato producers badly affected.

The sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) deal, largely agreed between the two sides in May , is due to be signed at next week’s summit. It will permit the removal of the vast majority of physical checks and most of the accompanying certificates and paperwork.

This will save businesses in the horticulture sector the current cost of trading with Europe , including plant health inspection fees, phytosanitary certificates, document and ID checks, port fees, agents’ fees, additional labour costs and extra haulage costs.

These costs total £60m a year, according to calculations by the industry body the Horticultural Trades Association (HTA), but do not include late delivery penalties or sales lost because of port delays or damage to goods.

These savings should put “downward pressure on food prices”, Eagle said, although she would not confirm the deal would lower the cost of food in the UK.

The promise of the deal was welcomed by Provender Nurseries, one of the UK’s largest wholesale nurseries, which sells thousands of plants, trees and shrubs to local authorities, parks and landscapers from its base at Swanley in Kent.

However, the company has already spent at least £500,000 on building a post-Brexit control post on its eight-hectare (20-acre) site, which will become obsolete once the deal is implemented.

Richard McKenna, the managing director of Provender, said the business constructed the “sealed building and bought four electric forklifts to operate in it” to allow inspections of lorry loads of valuable trees and shrubs imported from the continent.

The company decided to build the site to reduce the “delays and damage” it had experienced when smaller loads were inspected at government-run border control posts such as Sevington .

“It cost a lot for a barn, but it gave us security as a business,” said McKenna.

Despite this, McKenna hopes the SPS deal will convince some of Provender’s European suppliers, previously deterred by the paperwork and potential pitfalls of post-Brexit trade with the UK, to restart exports.

“We need to see the small print on the agreement,” he said. “It could have been sooner, but we are pleased that it is happening.”

The deal is not expected to be implemented until the first quarter of 2028, meaning businesses such as Provender will still be subject to the current border arrangements for more than a year.

In the meantime, Fran Barnes, the chief executive of the HTA, called for “some easements as a transition arrangement that are pragmatic” to help horticulture businesses, such as fewer or no checks on imports of lower-risk products.

Eagle conceded the implementation date was later than the mid-2027 targeted when the former prime minister Keir Starmer announced his EU “reset” deal in May 2025.

Starmer’s replacement by Andy Burnham led to a “pause” in negotiations with Brussels, said Eagle, with the upcoming November summit pushed back from July.

The original target was “always a very, very ambitious timescale,” she said. “That extra time has meant we could deal in a more coherent way with some of the knottier, thornier issues on things like pesticides.”

The UK has continued to use some pesticides and fungicides that are banned in the EU .

This has prompted industry concerns that British potatoes grown in 2027, treated with pesticides banned in the EU, could need to be thrown away if the resulting frozen chips went on sale after the deal’s implementation.

“We are very well aware of these kinds of issues and the EU is also very aware it doesn’t want to be seen to be wasting food,” Eagle said.

British exporters of produce including seed potatoes and some mussels also hope the SPS deal will allow trade halted by Brexit to restart.

“We have been waiting for this moment, but it all depends on the timing of the deal,” said Adam Taylor, a director of Taylors Bulbs in Lincolnshire, which supplies tulip, daffodil and other bulbs to garden centres and nurseries across the UK and Ireland.

A Brexit certification disagreement halted exports of British seed potatoes , particularly from Scotland, to the EU. Taylors underwent the “laborious and expensive” work of setting up an Irish business in order to keep supplying the Republic of Ireland.

“When things go back closer to how they were before Brexit, I hope our Irish customer base will reflect on the loyalty given to them,” he said.

items.lbText:
Increase reported by Aviva after Hastings Direct said claims were up 140% in August and Axa said it had been a ‘surge year’

The UK’s largest insurer has been hit by a rise in subsidence claims after an extremely hot summer left households across the country grappling with the fallout from the growing climate crisis.

Aviva said on Friday it had experienced the jump amid an industry-wide surge in households filing subsidence claims with their insurers to cover repairs, which typically are needed to address cracks, sloping floors, and off-kilter doors and windows.

It follows two record hot summers in the UK; August this year was the joint hottest month ever recorded around the world. Drier summers cause the ground under houses to shrink, which undermines a property’s foundations. It then expands in wetter winters, which can further damage homes.

Aviva experienced a “peak subsidence period” between July and September, with claims continuing into October, its chief executive, Amanda Blanc, told Bloomberg in an interview on Friday. Aviva would not provide any further detail on the scale of the increase in claims.

Blanc said homeowners could reduce the risk of subsidence by keeping a close eye on drains, pipes and gutters, and fixing any leaks that could affect the ground under homes. “It’s about managing trees and plumbing,” she said.

A number of fellow insurers have also experienced a rise in claims in recent months. Hastings Direct said it received record subsidence claims in August , up 140% compared with a year earlier. Axa, one of the UK’s biggest home insurers, has said it has been a “surge year” for subsidence.

The value of claims have also hit a record high. The average subsidence claim in the UK hit a high of £20,000 between April and June, more than £2,000 higher than a year earlier, according to the Association of British Insurers. Insurers paid out £72m for domestic subsidence claims, compared with £60m in the same period last year.

Millions of homes are at risk of subsidence because of the worsening climate crisis, according to the British Geological Survey, which estimates that up to 11% of UK homes – more than 4.2m houses – could be at risk by 2070. Older properties with shallow foundations and those built on clay-rich soil are facing the biggest threat, with areas including London, Essex, Kent and areas around Oxford among the most vulnerable.

But despite the rise in subsidence claims, Blanc said Aviva was in rude health, having reported a 19% rise in general insurance premiums to £11.8bn in the third quarter.

“Aviva is in great shape,” she said in a statement released alongside the company’s financial results. “Our performance has been excellent in the first nine months of 2026, demonstrating once again the benefits of scale across our diversified business. We continue to deliver strong, profitable growth, particularly in the capital-light areas of general insurance and wealth.”

items.lbText:
Supplies outstripped demand by almost 2m barrels a day in October as market shows ‘tentative signs of rebalancing’

The world’s oil supply is swinging back to a surplus for the first time since the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran, the International Energy Agency (IEA) has said.

Oil supplies outstripped demand by almost 2m barrels a day in October, the Paris-based agency said, as “Gulf exports recovered much faster than global oil demand”.

The market was “showing tentative signs of rebalancing, with global oil supplies surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran”, the IEA reported.

It comes after months of disruption to the global oil market as the Middle East conflict blocked shipments via the strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s oil and gas supply normally passes.

The conflict has triggered a rise in energy prices this year. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, traded at about $72 a barrel in February, before the conflict began, and hit $126 a barrel by the end of April.

However, this week prices fell to their lowest level since late August, at $89.66, after the US president, Donald Trump, told reporters that the war with Iran was “ effectively over ”. Brent crude was trading at about $95 a barrel on Friday.

There are still concerns around continued attacks on oil tankers in the Middle East, and this week reports emerged that senior Iranian officials believe the US could be planning further military strikes .

However, the IEA said it expected global oil supply to average 105m barrels a day in the final three months of the year, 1.7m higher than forecast demand. The agency had previously expected a deficit in the fourth quarter.

The recovery in global oil supplies has also eased pressure on emergency stockpiles, which have been diminished by the Iran conflict. The IEA said its members would speed up the release of remaining emergency oil stockpiles pledged earlier this year, adding a further 71m barrels to the market by the end of February. The stocks are held in refineries, oil terminals, power stations and at offshore fields in the North Sea.

The Opec+ oil cartel said this week that it had pumped 41m barrels a day of crude in October, up from about 2m in September and at 97% of its prewar volumes.

Global oil demand is also expected to fall by 2.68m barrels a day this year to 103.2m a day, the IEA reported. Consumption is forecast to rebound next year but is still expected to remain below 2025 levels, with growth mostly in petrochemical feed stocks as the market for vehicle fuel is hit by “high prices, electrification and fuel efficiency”.

items.title: The datacenter industry is using propaganda to fight opposition | Samuel Woolley, Dean Jackson and Maia Woluchem
items.author: Samuel Woolley, Dean Jackson and Maia Woluchem
items.content:
Big tech has used misdirection, disinformation and jargon to obscure the harm the facilities can cause to communities

“Antifa”. “Commies”. “Chinese bots”. Everyone from tech leaders to the president has called datacenter resistance a “documented psyop” and a “Chinese PR thing”.

But why do they make these claims? Our new research finds that the datacenter industry uses propaganda, disinformation, and information control to mold public opinion and undermine community opposition.

items.lbText:
Big tech has used misdirection, disinformation and jargon to obscure the harm the facilities can cause to communities

“Antifa”. “Commies”. “Chinese bots”. Everyone from tech leaders to the president has called datacenter resistance a “ documented psyop ” and a “ Chinese PR thing ”.

But why do they make these claims? Our new research finds that the datacenter industry uses propaganda, disinformation, and information control to mold public opinion and undermine community opposition.

Big tech’s opening pitch about datacenters was typical: they told Americans that these facilities brought jobs and tax revenue . They spread this message through mailers , text messages , TV spots and targeted digital ads .

But much of the spending behind these multimedia campaigns flowed through opaque non-profits and dark money groups with tech industry ties, hiding the source of these efforts. Groups like “ Elevate New Mexico ” have passed themselves off as local initiatives while obscuring their connections to corporate entities in the datacenter space.

As environmental concerns mounted, the industry turned to misdirection and jargon to obscure datacenters’ impact.

Developers continue to use terms such as “ closed-loop cooling ” and “ behind-the-meter power ” to deflect concerns about water and power consumption. But while these approaches can mitigate consumption, the effect is smaller than often implied: closed-loop systems may simply shift demand for water up the supply chain to power plants, while behind-the-meter generators still rely on the grid for backup and stability while competing with it for components.

And those industry figures about job creation? They are often presented without any context.

To give an example, an ad by Build American AI – an industry advocacy group connected to Lead the Future, an industry Pac funded by OpenAI and Andreessen Horowitz – boasts that datacenters have created 57,785 jobs in Texas.

But industry figures can also be misleading: of the promised jobs, how many are permanent jobs remaining after construction? How many are cafeteria workers, landscapers, and custodial staff – who often work for subcontractors without benefits? And are those subcontractors included when industry reports the average salaries for the jobs they do create?

A similar story applies to other tax benefits. When companies mention the tax revenue they bring to communities, they rarely include the exemptions and abatements they received.

Those incentives are often unnecessary to attract projects and eat directly into budgets for schools and social services. Some jurisdictions even track the precise number of dollars they forgo through such abatements.

But even when agreements allow communities to claw back money from underperforming projects, local leaders are often hesitant to do so because they don’t want to admit a project has failed. In other words, accountability is rare.

The industry fights to keep critical details about projects under wraps, sometimes working with local authorities to do so. In The Dalles, Oregon, for example, Google paid the city’s legal fees after it withheld records about a datacenter’s water use. (The city agreed to release the information in a settlement with the Oregonian newspaper.) Most datacenters do not report their water consumption at all, hampering policymaking. As for the public, their visibility into the process is limited by non-disclosure agreements.

Local and state officials, operating in a low-information environment and starved of resources by anti-tax policies, welcomed these facilities at first. The public has been more skeptical. With time, some government officials have joined them.

Yet, local organizers and activists told us that they now see decisions about their economic future as pre-determined by big business and opaque governments. They criticized the lack of transparency, the late stage at which the public was consulted, and community benefits agreements they felt were inadequate compared to the burdens they were being asked to bear: higher electric costs, air pollution, noise, water depletion, and a change in the character of their communities.

Industrial tycoons have historically manipulated leaders, laws, and regulations to their advantage. This time, though, resistance has been fierce.

Perhaps that is why the industry has stooped to smearing its opponents as useful stooges of foreign propaganda. In May, Kevin O’Leary – the millionaire Shark Tank star who is developing one of the world’s largest datacenters – called two activists “proxies for the Chinese government”. He later admitted he had “ no evidence ”. Even so, similar theories have gained traction among tech executives and Washington policymakers. And it has percolated to the local level, where activists and organizers tell us they face this invective – and much more – online.

The irony is that datacenter proponents are often the ones relying on disinformation and other information manipulation tactics to make their case. Government decision-makers should not give credence to top-down claims from Silicon Valley or the broader datacenter industry suggesting community opposition is somehow propelled by China.

Instead, policymakers should create and enforce mandatory transparency requirements and other provisions forcing datacenters to keep their promises and provide critical data about resource consumption, job creation and other matters of public concern. Those transparency requirements should extend to the permissive environment for advertising and campaign finance in which disinformation and coordinated astroturf movements thrive.

As usual, sunlight is the best disinfectant.

Samuel Woolley is the Dietrich chair of disinformation studies and directs the Communication Technology Research Lab (CTRL) at the University of Pittsburgh

Dean Jackson is a senior fellow at the Communication Technology Research Lab and a contributing editor at Tech Policy Press…

items.lbText:
Ministers consider banning under-16s from online marketplaces amid reported misuse of messaging functions and users’ photos

In June, Hannah* listed her seven-year-old daughter’s pink swimming costume for sale on Vinted, hoping other parents surfing the reselling site would snap up the £1 offer. Her inbox pinged.

“So a little girl wore this yh [yeah]?” wrote a user with a male handle.

After sending back a barbed “What do you think?”, Hannah swiftly blocked the user and reported the incident to Vinted. She described the exchange as “disgusting” and “disturbing”.

Her experience is just one of the many innocuous listings of children and young people’s secondhand clothes on reselling apps that are attracting sexualised comments through their direct messaging function.

The Children’s Society has said some young users of resale sites are increasingly being asked for indecent photos in exchange for money or gifts. Some photos of young users posted on the platforms have been AI deepfaked into nudes without their consent.

In response, ministers are considering banning under-16s from platforms such as Depop, eBay and Facebook Marketplace, according to the Sunday Times , over mounting fears that their private messaging functions are the latest frontline in child exploitation. Vinted, which has a minimum age of 18, would have to join the other sites in gating access with strict age verification features.

The culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, said on Sunday that the government was “looking seriously” at expanding the under-16s social media ban to include online marketplaces. It is understood the regulations were sent for cabinet signoff this week, with Nandy expected to present them to parliament in December.

Young women have posted on TikTok and Reddit about their concerning interactions with buyers. Those exchanges include asking the seller if the item will come with used underwear if they buy it, or unsolicited sexual comments about their appearance.

Lucy* started reselling her pre-loved clothes on Depop when she was 15 and has been subject to many unsettling experiences. Once, she listed an item of clothing for about £10 and a user requested to raise the price. “The person had changed it to £30 and said: ‘If you include your pants I’ll pay more’,” she said. “That made me feel like, oh my God, awful.”

She then discovered that images of her taken when she was under the age of 18, posted to advertise her clothes, had been scraped from Depop and were circulating on Reddit.

“These pictures are actually still being resurfaced on these Reddit pages, which is quite frustrating,” she said. “It would be me at 17 trying to sell a bikini, and these men have screenshotted these images … It’s not just me, it’s hundreds of other girls.”

About two years ago, Lucy came across another social media platform, Discord, where she found users had stolen her old Vinted and Depop photos and manipulated them using AI to make deepfakes of her “fully nude”. She said: “It’s deplorable that people think it’s acceptable to take people’s images and make them into AI porn – I felt really, really upset.”

Vinted says minors can only access the site under the supervision of adult account holders, while Depop says users must be aged 13 or over to set up an account, and over 18 to use PayPal and the Depop payment systems. However, the UK communications watchdog, Ofcom, has found that 15% of eight to 14-year-olds use Vinted each month, while another report has suggested that some children are able to bypass checks and access age-restricted online services.

Some child safety campaigners have expressed fears a sweeping social media ban could exclude children from the internet entirely. Karen Garland, the head of policy at the Marie Collins Foundation, a charity that supports victims of technology-assisted child sexual exploitation, said: “We need to make spaces for children and young people that are safer by design. And so, in some ways, extending a ban into other spaces may not be the best route overall.”

Despite her experience, Lucy is conflicted about the ban. “It’s a real shame because there are probably very young girls that maybe are from different backgrounds … that maybe really need that money.”

However, she acknowledged that there could be “extremely dangerous” consequences to selling clothes on Vinted. She said that as she was now 25 and has continued to find sexualised images of herself online,, the risk did not end at 18.

A Vinted spokesperson said: “We have zero tolerance for harmful or explicit content and use a combination of dedicated moderation teams and detection tools to spot and remove activity that breaks our rules. When we identify inappropriate behaviour, we take action, up to a permanent ban or reporting to the relevant authorities.”

An eBay spokesperson said: “We have clear policies and safeguards to protect our community, including encouraging people to keep conversations on eBay, avoid sharing personal contact details and report any suspicious or inappropriate behaviour. Where we or our customers identify policy violations, we take appropriate action.”

Depop said: “Using someone’s images without their permission is a violation of our terms of service , which explicitly prohibits users from using or sharing another user’s content without their consent, whether on Depop or elsewhere. We take the safety of our community extremely seriously and we have robust policies, controls and processes in place to protect our users.”

items.lbText:
One company is proposing elongating the life of the dump, pungent smell and all, several more decades

A s a visual representation of how New York is running out of places to put its waste, the largest active landfill in the state is a striking one. The hulking Seneca Meadows landfill is already the height of the Statue of Liberty and its operators are seeking to raise it even further, to the consternation of nearby residents.

The landfill, situated in the scenic Finger Lakes region in the northern reaches of New York state, has grown since the 1980s to now sprawl across 350 acres of deposited trash, mounded up to the height of around 300ft – roughly the same height of the Statue of Liberty.

“All around the lakes is pretty flat until you see this monster of a hill,” said Mark Pitifer, a marketing administrator at Waterloo Containers, a glass packaging company that sits next to the landfill and is dwarfed by its neighbor. “I mean it’s incredible, it’s like being in downtown New York City only instead of a building, it’s trash.”

Locals in the nearby towns of Waterloo and Seneca Falls, the latter famed as the birthplace of the women’s rights movement in the US, had hoped the bulging landfill would be closed when its permit expired last year. But the operator, Texas-based Waste Connections, has proposed elongating the life of the landfill for several more decades via 47 acres of newly lined disposal cells and adding another 70ft to the trash heap’s height.

As New York state authorities mull whether to grant this expansion, the landfill has become a central point of grievance over the pungent smell, water pollution and planet-heating pollution given off by the places we dump our rubbish. Seneca Meadows is now the largest source of methane, a potent greenhouse gas, in the state, according to a study last year based on researchers using aircraft measurements.

The operator, Waste Connections, did not respond to questions from the Guardian; it defends its environmental protections measures and record in statements on its website.

The increasing size of landfills also raises uncomfortable questions about how much waste we produce and what to do with it. Seneca Meadows receives around 6,000 tons of trash each day from across New York, with 1,500 of those tons originating from New York City, which sends its rubbish to landfills hundreds of miles away that are rapidly filling up and are set to be completely full within the next 16 to 25 years .

If burning rubbish or casually dumping it into rivers and the ocean is too environmentally harmful, what is to be done with our waste beyond continually supersizing landfills to the point they become a major climate , as well as local, hazard?

“We are at the precipice of a crisis,” said Emily Gallagher, a Democratic member of the New York state assembly who recently took a tour of the Seneca Meadows site and has convened a hearing on the state’s waste storage policies.

“There is this huge mountain of trash that is off gassing almost 24 hours a day … contaminating the Finger Lakes, contaminating the groundwater,” she said of the site. “People we met in town are in really bad shape, we need to shut this expansion attempt down now.”

Gallagher said intense lobbying and donations from interests aligned with the plastics and fossil fuels industries has stymied strict measures to reduce waste and enforce more recycling – she estimated 80% of the Seneca Meadows contents could be recycled. But she added there needed to be a broader societal reckoning with the tsunami of trash, much of it from cheap and disposal items, we create.

“We say throwing away but there is no away,” said Gallagher, whose district includes a part of New York City’s borough of Brooklyn. “The problem is that it will take a culture change that people won’t want to do until it is forced in their faces. We used to have a much more circular economy, where people reused and rewashed everything, but we have been indoctrinated into a convenience culture, even if it then causes us more inconvenience.”

Dealing with trash is “gross problem”, Gallagher acknowledged. “But we need a much deeper conversation about it rather than continuously pushing it to the side because it’s uncomfortable and it confronts our human desire for comfort and our laziness,” she added.

The municipal government of New York City has pointed to recent efforts to reduce its waste, such as the pickup and composting of organic matter, which makes up around a third of what is left as trash in the city.

Yet New York City residents still create around 12,000 tons of trash a day and it will need to go somewhere. The city does not send residential trash to Seneca Meadows – although some private contractors do – but will be sending it further and further from the city, which has not hosted its own waste for several decades.

“As capacity continues to shrink in the region, we will likely export trash to further locations,” said a spokesman for the city’s sanitation department. “Our commitment to rail export makes this much easier than trucking.”

Yvonne Taylor, co-founder of Seneca Lake Guardian environmental group, stressed she didn’t want other communities to suffer living near growing landfills like hers had.

Residents routinely text her to say that they have had to remove their children from the nearby school because the smell had sickened them, or of ruined outdoor birthday parties and other gatherings, she said. Pitifer, of Waterloo Containers, said the company has had to install filtration equipment to help employees deal with the overpowering stench of the landfill.

“We don’t need to use plastic grocery bags, we don’t need to use plastic toothbrushes, toothpaste, shampoo bottles, and laundry detergent bottles – all of those things can be packaged in other materials that don’t wind up in a landfill,” said Taylor.…

items.lbText:
Eccentric and overhyped, Tesla’s Cybertruck became a stand-in for Elon Musk during his ascent in the Republican party. It will join the ranks of other vehicles symbolic of their eras – for better or for worse

Three days after a historic blue tsunami changed America’s political landscape, Elon Musk announced Tesla would end production of its hulking Cybertruck next year.

Was it a coincidence? Maybe. Musk said the move was “to make room for increased Cybercab production”, referring to Tesla’s Robotaxi. But the combined circumstances felt highly appropriate: it was the end of an era.

Eccentric and overhyped, the Cybertruck became a kind of automotive stand-in for Musk himself amid his political ascent. Like so many of his projects, it was massively promoted, heavily delayed, and ultimately fell short: Musk once predicted he could sell 250,000 a year but ultimately sold 70,000 in three years , losing $1.9bn in the process, according to Quartz.

The design seemed to prioritize science fiction over robust engineering: the unveiling was in November 2019, when the film Blade Runner was set , as Musk proudly pointed out – but it didn’t arrive on the roads until four years later. At that unveiling event, Musk infamously showed off the Cybertruck’s durability by having a designer throw a ball at its window, which cracked. While Musk called it apocalypse-proof , it often seemed like the opposite: Cybertrucks suffered at least five vehicle fires , four of them deadly – making them deadlier than the notorious Ford Pinto, according to an analysis . They were subject to 11 recalls amid technical issues, including a loose pedal that could get stuck and cause unintentional acceleration. They routinely got stuck in the snow .

Like its creator, the Cybertruck was highly divisive. Many observers were repulsed by its bizarre, boxy appearance and its road-hogging size (a parallel parking nightmare). “It is the ugliest vehicle I think I have ever laid eyes on,” the automotive expert Mike Caudill told Fox Business . Others, however, were deeply devoted to their Cybertrucks. “I’ve got 6,000 miles on my Cybertruck; I’ve had zero issues,” Matt Holm, president of the Tesla Owners Club of Austin, told the Houston Chronicle .

Indeed, the Cybertruck had its strong points, according to experts. “People at Tesla were rightly proud of the engineering they put into it,” said Ezra Dyer, a senior editor and columnist at Car and Driver . But “a lot of the engineering problems they solved were self-imposed” – driven by the need to incorporate Musk’s super-epic design choices.

“Why is that important to you that it be bulletproof?” Jay Leno asked Musk during a test drive. “Because it’s badass and super cool,” the CEO replied.

All this, of course, coincided with Musk’s political rise in the Trump administration. The truck, as the Guardian’s Andrew Lawrence put it, became essentially “a Maga hat on wheels”, indicating its driver’s political beliefs – or at least the politics onlookers would ascribe to them. The archetypal Cybertruck driver was a guy, “probably with some kind of goatee, likely compensating for something, so desperate for attention that he will take negative attention”, as an automotive analyst told the New York Times. Many drivers of various Tesla models rushed to distance themselves from the CEO with bumper stickers that say, “I bought this before Elon went crazy.”

The Cybertruck, meanwhile, “became this totem and symbol of Elon Musk himself”, says Dan Neil, an auto columnist for the Wall Street Journal.

While Cybertrucks took to the streets, Musk was taking a literal chainsaw to the US government as head of the department of government efficiency (Doge), which bore plenty of similarities to the truck, beginning with the empty promises. Musk said Doge could cut $2tn from the federal budget; its website now claims it has cut just $215bn. In the process, hundreds of thousands of workers left the government due to workforce reductions, early retirement and other reasons – before, in a move reminiscent of the Cybertruck’s recalls, many were rehired. And like the Cybertruck, it all came to an embarrassing end: Musk left government under a cloud as he feuded with Donald Trump over spending in his “big, beautiful bill”.

Now, when it comes to the Cybertruck, “you’ve got this expensive luxury product with a very off-putting aesthetic and all this political baggage,” Dyer says (the 2026 model runs from about $72,000 to $102,000 ). So it’s little surprise that sales have struggled. “It’s following the trajectory of any cult vehicle,” Dyer says. The hardcore fans line up, but once they’ve all got theirs, demand fizzles.

As it reaches the end of its short road, the Cybertruck – outwardly mighty, inwardly fragile, a poorly conceived product of an increasingly oligarchical system – feels alarmingly apt as a symbol of Trump 2.0 Phase I. Ten years from now, spotting an ageing Cybertruck on the street will serve as a reminder of the bad old days.

It will join the ranks of other vehicles symbolic of their eras – for better or for worse.

The Cybertruck is to the 2020s what the Volkswagen Transporter – AKA the VW Bus – is to the 1960s. In many ways, the two are opposites: the VW Bus calls forth images of peace and music, flower decals, and a crowd of well-meaning hippies packed inside. Sixty years after the summer of love, the Cybertruck suggests an isolated middle-aged man hiding from the apocalypse.

The vehicles do have a few things in common, however. One is drugs, but while the VW conjures cannabis, the Cybertruck is more ketamine. The other is a reputation for putting looks over safety.

A few decades later came another icon of its era – in many ways the progenitor to the Cybertruck: the Hummer H2, introduced in the early 2000s. Like the Cybertruck, the Hummer was inconveniently enormous and associated with a certain kind of aggressive masculinity.…

items.lbText:
Bournemouth became a hub for thousands of finance jobs after the 1980s big bang, but new tech risks hurting Dorset’s economy

A few minutes’ drive from Bournemouth’s sandy beachfront, on the site of a former farm, lies an unlikely nerve centre of international finance. Here, miles from the glass towers of London’s Canary Wharf, more than 5,300 staff including compliance officers, analysts and software engineers help process more than $1tn (£750bn) worth of global transactions each day for the largest US bank, JP Morgan.

The sprawling five-hectare (13-acre) campus, which hosted just 650 workers when it opened in 1986, has solidified Dorset’s status as one of Britain’s largest financial hubs outside London.

Now, the financial services industry accounts for 10% of the county’s turnover – the total revenue generated by all businesses in the area – with 2,500 companies, including Nationwide Building Society, the insurer LV=, and the asset manager Canaccord Wealth, collectively employing 24,000 staff, according to the Dorset Chamber of Commerce.

But along with other regional finance centres outside London, from Leeds to Birmingham, and Swindon to Cardiff, it faces an existential threat from AI.

Bosses are considering how the technology can help automate costly human-led jobs, putting at risk a swathe of back-office roles, such as data processors, compliance checkers and entry-level analysts.

The Barclays chief executive, CS Venkatakrishnan, last month announced 5,000 job cuts linked to advances in AI , while another London-headquartered bank, Standard Chartered, said in May it was planning to slash 7,000 roles as it doubled down on artificial intelligence.

AI now poses the biggest threat to the UK’s financial workforce since the 2008 financial crisis, says Caren Evans, a national officer for the Unite union, referring to an era when banks needed multibillion-pound taxpayer bailouts and subsequently embarked on swingeing cost cuts.

Unite members, who include staff at NatWest, Lloyds and Barclays , are “very very worried about AI”, Evans says. “They’re worried about losing their job, they’re worried about having future skills, they’re worried about having sustainable careers.”

All that is hitting staff morale. One Barclays employee said they felt “very undervalued and insignificant”, adding: “It’s kind of hard to be enthusiastic about your work when you know, at any moment, senior executives are thinking about how to get rid of you. You’re not seen as an asset, you’re seen as a problem to be removed.”

The JP Morgan chief executive, Jamie Dimon, has warned of the fallout from AI, saying widespread job losses could spark “civil unrest” unless governments and business supported displaced workers. He said retraining programmes, and even state-sponsored wage support, relocation schemes and early retirement could be needed to ease the blow.

In Dorset, the banking tech push has already left its mark, with bosses closing Barclays House in Poole in 2022 after 46 years of operation. “It was the original site that all the cheques in the country used to go through, to be checked,” Gareth Sherwood, the president of the Dorset Chamber of Commerce, says. “And of course, that went with digitisation.” That office block still stands empty today.

Sherwood’s organisation has been coaching local business to embrace AI and increase productivity. “There’s winners and losers in all change,” he says. But “we would still encourage people to use human beings”, both to support local jobs, but also mitigate cybersecurity risks and unplanned outages. “You can’t switch a human off in the same way that you can switch an AI off,” he adds.

But if cost-cutting bank bosses start to axe back office roles at pace, there would be ripple effects throughout regional economies such as Dorset. Demand for professional support from law firms and consultancies could start to dry up, and the wider ecosystem of services, such as gyms, hairdressers, restaurants and estate agents, could start to suffer. “The collateral would be to some of the more service aspects of [the economy],” Sherwood says. “And it’s hard enough to keep young people in this area.”

The Conservative councillor Lawrence Williams has served Littledown and Iford, the ward hosting JP Morgan’s campus, since 2011. He originally moved to the area in the early 1980s, shortly before the bank – then known as Chase Manhattan – took up its lodgings on former farmland.

The 76-year-old regularly meets JP Morgan bosses, but says he has heard nothing of AI-related job cuts. The bank itself says the Bournemouth campus is a “centre for financial innovation”, adding: “AI will enable us to do more, and we train our people to make the most of it.”

But if companies start to follow in Barclays’ and Standard Chartered’s footsteps, that “could hit quite hard”, particularly for an economy otherwise reliant on seasonal tourism, Williams says.

Bournemouth originally developed as a health and wellness destination for Victorian-era medical patients, which makes it a bit of an outlier amid other regional finance hubs across the UK, whose roots are more closely tied to the Industrial Revolution.

In the late 1800s, banks and insurers congregated around big industry, providing loans and services to Birmingham’s engineering firms, Manchester’s cotton sector, Leeds’ wool operations and Newcastle’s shipbuilding industry. By 1873, approximately four-fifths of the banks in England and Wales were headquartered outside London. (Edinburgh was of course a big financial centre in its own right, but was unique in that companies kept decision-making centralised in the Scottish city.)

Those hubs continued to grow until the latter half of the 20th century, when postwar deindustrialisation took hold, reducing local demand for financing.…

Exclusive: Fossil fuels no longer dominant energy source, IEA leader says, as summit considers electrification pledge

The world has left behind the age of coal, oil and gas and is now firmly in “the age of electricity”, the world’s leading energy economist has said.

Fatih Birol, the executive director of the International Energy Agency (IEA), said more than twice as much electricity generation would be added to the global economy in the next decade than in the last, as countries scramble to secure their energy supplies against fossil fuel price volatility and supply shocks, such as the Iran war.

Transport is being electrified at an unprecedented rate: outside China, sales of electric cars have risen by 60% in the last nine months, the IEA has found. The growth of AI datacentres is also spurring electricity generation, as is the rapid growth in air conditioning, according to Birol, as heatwaves grow more intense and more frequent under rising global temperatures.

“We will still use oil and gas, but the dominant source of energy is becoming electricity,” Birol told the Guardian in an interview at the Cop31 UN climate summit in Turkey . “One staggering number [is that] in the last 10 years, the world has added about 5,000 gigawatts of electricity. And we expect, in a very conservative way, in the next 10 years, about 12,000 gigawatts, more than two times more than what we had in the last 10 years.”

Governments from 185 countries are meeting this week and next in Antalya for the annual talks, where the turn to electrification in place of fossil fuels is one of the key topics. A resolution to derive 35% of final energy worldwide from electricity by 2035 is on the table, which if it succeeds, could be one of the most important ways of achieving the needed decarbonisation of economies by mid-century.

Electricity now fulfils about a quarter of most energy needs while three-quarters of final energy worldwide is supplied by fossil fuels , mostly for transport, heating and industrial uses. Global electricity was increasingly generated by renewable sources and that process would speed up even faster over the next decades, Birol said.

The more our lives can be powered by clean energy the better, say experts, not least because, as a result of the inefficiency of fossil fuels , most of the rest of our energy is wasted as heat, so when these activities are electrified, only about half of the energy needs to be replaced.

Most countries back the electrification goal, according to Birol. He has worked closely with the Turkish and Australian governments, which are jointly presiding over this year’s summit . “It will be an unmistakable signal to the markets and investors that governments see that the future of energy is in electricity,” he said. “This will make the age of electricity even earlier and cheaper. It might be one of the most consequential decisions coming from Cops in the last several years.”

But even if the resolution was not adopted – some governments, including Saudi Arabia and Russia, are said to be opposed, and owing to the convention by which consensus is needed to pass decisions, a small number of countries can hold the rest to ransom – the “staggering” progress would continue, Birol said.

“The reason is there are three major drivers for electrification: one is AI and datacentres; second is the electrification transportation sector; and third, the most important one in terms of volume, is air conditioning. Air conditioners are growing explosively,” he said.

In the US, about 90% of households have access to air conditioning, but in India it is fewer than 20%, and in Nigeria about 5%. “With the increasing effects of climate change, and if they have more money, [people] buy air conditioners,” said Birol. “These things are happening, and electrification is not bad. It is good for energy security, because it is your own electricity [generated within a country rather than imported, as fossil fuels often are], good for the competitiveness of countries, and good for climate change.”

He added: “Global energy demand is growing strongly, but global electricity demand is growing three times faster than total energy demand. And it is impossible to stop it. The one and only issue is making electricity affordable for people.”

Birol placed the blame for the UK’s high electricity prices firmly on gas. “There is always a debate about this in the UK, but in fact the single most important reason why UK electricity prices may be on the high side is reliance on imported gas. Gas prices went up, so did the electricity prices, full stop. And the solution is not importing more gas, but building more [renewable] electricity at home,” he said.

The transformation is happening fast. “Five years ago, only 5% of all the cars sold was electric. And this year, we expect it is about one-third of all the cars sold is electric, and electric trucks are coming. This is going to displace a significant amount of oil ,” he said.

“If the electrification pledge comes out [of Cop31] and the countries decide that the world’s energy future is electric, then it will definitely lead to a secure, more affordable and more livable planet.”

items.lbText:
Owning an electric car, driving an electric motorbike taxi, riding scooters – we speak to people in Oslo, Kigali and Shanghai about their everyday routines

T he race to electrification has emerged as a key theme of this year’s UN climate summit: increasing the use of electricity – particularly from clean sources – has the potential to improve daily life for people around the world.

The summit’s co-hosts are now trying to get countries to promise to increase their electricity use to 35% of all energy used by 2035. The global figure currently stands at 23%, but some countries are already striding ahead. As 100,000 delegates, negotiators and world leaders thrash out the details in Antalya, Turkey , the Guardian spoke to three people in Norway, Rwanda and China to find out what life looks like in more highly electrified countries.

Norway is a world leader in the race to 100% electrification. In September, a record 98.81% of new cars sold were electric, and hydropower produces 90% of all electricity . But with rapidly rising energy demands, including from new datacentres, authorities warn that the country could soon face a power deficit and higher energy prices.

Unni Berge, 47, lives in Oslo with her husband and two teenage sons and works as the head of communications at the Norwegian EV Association. She describes how electricity features in a typical day:

“I use electricity in my three-bedroom flat and I have district heating [where heat is transported around a local network from a centralised source rather than individual boilers to heat homes and buildings]. For electricity we are connected to the Norwegian central grid, which is mainly hydropower.

“I live in a rather energy-efficient flat, so our electricity bills are comparatively low. In October, we spent 730 Norwegian kroner [£57] on electricity for our apartment, and in September it was 500 kroner.

“I go to work by bus. Almost all the buses in Oslo are fully electric. I also have an electric car, but driving in the middle of Oslo for work is not an option because we have a lot of restrictions on cars in the city centre. In my street, the bus comes every fifth minute, so I don’t have to plan. I go outside and a bus comes.

“I mostly use my electric car on weekends. A lot of the trips are driving to sports activities with my two children, who are 18 and 15. I also train a handball team, so I use it to go to a lot of handball matches and tournaments.

“We charge our car with a charging box in our garage where, like most apartment garages in Oslo, we have built a collective charging system. If everyone put their charging on at the same time it would go slow, but in practice that doesn’t happen.

“I have a large battery on my EV so I charge it once every two to three weeks. Of course we pay for the electricity and a system fee, but it’s much cheaper than petrol and diesel.

“In my office, we have district heating, which is quite common in Oslo in larger buildings, then we use electricity for light and computers. Lunch is made in my office in the internal canteen with electricity. At work I use Microsoft Copilot, which is a really helpful tool, but of course there are big questions there – energy demands will get too high if everyone is using AI more.

“I come home and use electricity to make dinner, watch television and go to the cinema. Growing up in a small village on the western coast of Norway , we also used wood for heating as well as electricity. But it is fair to say that electricity is common part of Norwegian life and has been for a long time.

“What has changed is that our transport sector is also now run on a rising amount of electricity: passenger cars, buses and also ferries. That happened quite fast. Heavy goods vehicles are also increasingly electric, so of course that changes the system and society.

“Perhaps because of the war in Ukraine and more extreme weather conditions, people are becoming aware that they are quite dependent on electricity, so in recent years there has been debate on how to prepare for a crisis. In previous power cuts, some people have used their electric cars as a battery to power electric equipment.

“There is also a big debate about electricity prices. In Norway we have nearly 100% renewable electricity, but even so we are connected to the European grid. So the gas prices still influence our electricity prices. And when we have dry winters, electricity prices rise because if we have less snow, the hydropower gets less water. Rising numbers of datacentres is also something consumers are starting to wonder about – what this development is going to look like and how much energy it is using.”

Six years ago, the Rwandan government embarked on an enthusiastic promotion of e-mobility by removing a number of taxes on e-bikes and vehicles and offering incentives for businesses operating charging stations.

The government has also banned registration of new fossil fuel-powered motorcycles in Kigali, the capital and Rwanda’s largest city, and is prioritising EVs in its vehicle acquisition.

Claver Habagusenga is an e-motorbike taxi driver living in Kigali. He shares a typical day:

“My day begins at 5am and ends late in the evening. My first job is a general clean of my bike, checking tyre pressure, seeing if the brakes are in order, verifying battery health. I have come to learn that riding on Rwandan roads requires strict discipline, as traffic regulations are strictly enforced and a breach attracts heavy fines.

“In the last five years, I have learned to prepare my breakfast using an induction cooker. In the past, I used to use a charcoal stove, which would delay my food and my work. Besides, a charcoal stove would affect my entire family with heavy smoke, and also cost me heavily in fuel each day.…

items.title: Who is Colette Kress, interim Nvidia CEO after Jensen Huang exit?

items.lbText:
Chief financial officer, reportedly disparaged by Huang during summer meeting, to take over on short-term basis

The hunt is on for a new Nvidia CEO. It comes after a whirlwind week, which saw the company head and co-founder, Jensen Huang, resign amid multiple allegations of extramarital affairs , including one that involved an alleged Chinese spy and two with company employees.

Nvidia immediately named Colette Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, as the interim CEO. It’s possible she could stay on permanently, but the company could also name another candidate for the full-time role. Names that have been floated include Ian Buck, who manages Nvidia’s AI hardware and software products, and Rene Haas, a former Nvidia employee and the current CEO of Arm Holdings, a UK-based chipmaker.

Whoever takes over from Huang will have tremendous sway in the burgeoning world of artificial intelligence. The entire AI ecosphere relies on Nvidia, which engineers advanced chips used to train AI models and power companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. Nvidia is also a central driver of the US economy and one of the world’s most valuable companies, with a market cap of around $4tn.

Huang, who co-founded the company in 1993, is known as an ambitious and visionary CEO who had a hand in most all aspects of the business. He led in an unusual management style, having about 60 direct reports, giving him more control over the company’s daily functions. His son and daughter also work at Nvidia, with his daughter seen as his possible proxy, but neither appear to have sufficient experience to take the helm.

Kress, 59, joined Nvidia in 2013 as the CFO after working in finance roles at Texas Instruments, Microsoft and Cisco. She’s a regular contributor to the company’s quarterly earnings calls, and has overseen Nvidia go from a niche firm geared toward video game chips to a trillion-dollar AI juggernaut. People who know her describe Kress as a calming contrast to Huang’s often confrontational style, Reuters reported.

“Colette has helped lead Nvidia through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position,” Harvey C Jones, the newly named chair of Nvidia’s board of directors, said in a statement on Thursday. “The board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team.”

But that sentiment may not be shared by Huang. During a meeting this past summer, the CEO said Kress was “a deer in the headlights” and interrupted her presentation, a person familiar with the comments told the Wall Street Journal . Huang insinuated during that August meeting that Kress was not someone who could help him make decisions.

However, Kress praised Huang in a memo to employees on Thursday, saying she would continue “building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years”.

Many investors, analysts and industry sources who spoke to Reuters questioned whether a finance executive could preserve the technological risk-taking that turned Nvidia into an AI chips powerhouse.

“Putting [Kress] in the interim role makes sense to keep the markets calm, but I don’t think she is the long-term visionary that Nvidia needs to continue its current trajectory,” said Anshel Sag, principal analyst at Moor Insights and Strategy.

Kress, who said in her memo that Nvidia’s “strength has always come from its people” , will serve as both the CEO and interim CFO until the board names a permanent successor.

The board said it was starting a search for Huang’s permanent replacement and is considering internal and external candidates. Along with Kress, Buck is seen as a possible successor. He has worked at Nvidia since 2004 and in charge of deploying generative AI in partnership with the world’s top AI companies, including Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta, OpenAI and more.

Haas, the CEO of Arm Holdings, is also well-known at Nvidia, having worked there for seven years as a vice president and general manager before joining Arm in 2013. Lisa Su, the CEO of chipmaker AMD, is also being named as a possible replacement for Huang. Her company is Nvidia’s most direct and fierce competitor; she’s also a distant cousin to Huang.

Sunny Cheung, an analyst at the Washington-based Jamestown Foundation, said Kress could face congressional questions about the company’s oversight of chip sales involving Chinese military-linked institutions and south-east Asian intermediaries.

In a 2023 interview with an Israeli publication, Kress credited her two young sons with urging her to join Nvidia in 2013 because they knew its chips from their video games.

She became a billionaire in 2025 based on the value of her Nvidia equity, according to media reports, and Forbes said her net worth of $1.2 billion in mid-2026 put her in 32nd place on its list of America’s richest self-made women.

Kress, who holds an undergraduate degree in finance and an MBA, was also named among the 50 most powerful women in business on rankings compiled by Fortune and Forbes magazines in recent years.

Nvidia’s CEO turmoil comes as the company is set to report its third-quarter earnings next Tuesday.

Kalshi announces ‘mutual decision’ as Democrats say they plan to investigate Trump family’s investments

Donald Trump Jr is no longer a paid adviser for Kalshi, the prediction market company said Thursday.

Kalshi described it as a mutual business decision between the two parties that followed a decision by Trump Jr’s investment firm, 1789 Capital, to increase its investment in Kalshi’s biggest competitor Polymarket.

But the announcement comes a week after Democrats were able to take control of both the House and Senate in the midterm elections.

Democrats have said they planned to investigate the Trump family’s investments, including their business relationships with both prediction markets.

“We have mutually agreed to end Don’s advisory role after his firm’s significant investment in a competitor this past summer,” said Dani Lever, a spokesperson for Kalshi. “We are grateful for his contributions in helping us market Kalshi to more customers.”

The president’s eldest son became a paid “strategic adviser” for Kalshi shortly after President Trump was sworn into office for his second term in January 2025 and has been an investor in Polymarket since August 2025. Both companies have seen their popularity and use jump significantly in the past two years.

At the same time, both companies have received favorable treatment from the White House. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission has backed the industry’s efforts to expand their products nationwide, including allowing their customers to trade sports-related contracts.

Both companies have adamantly denied that the financial relationship between Polymarket, Kalshi and the Trumps played any role in how the industry has been regulated under this administration.

1789 Capital increased its investment in Polymarket this past August, as part of Polymarket’s latest fundraising round. It was this investment that started the conversation about ending Trump Jr’s advisory role with Kalshi.

The prime minister was meeting fellow leaders at the European Political Community summit in Dublin, ahead of a keenly anticipated EU-UK summit next week, where he hopes to bring Britain closer to Europe.
