items.lbText:
Prime minister says reset could be a deal ‘like the Brexit people thought they were voting for in 2016’

Andy Burnham has said he believes a “win-win” deal could be done with the EU that could be “more like the Brexit that people thought they were voting for in 2016”.

The prime minister was meeting fellow leaders at the European Political Community summit in Dublin, ahead of a keenly anticipated EU-UK summit next week, where he hopes to bring Britain closer to Europe .

At the bilateral summit the EU and UK hope to sign deals on food and drink, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme, but the question of tuition fees for European students remains a stumbling block.

Burnham said: “I believe there is a good deal to be done that could be a win-win for Britain and Europe.

“The deal is not done, and there’ll be some long nights ahead in the next seven days.”

He said the reset would be about whether we can “take a step back to closer working relationships with Europe”.

Burnham added: “We ended up with a far harder Brexit , I think, than people thought they were getting when they went to the polls.”

The EU has said the prized food and drink deal and emissions-trading agreement may not enter into force without a deal on tuition fees in which European students would pay domestic rates.

Burnham said it was a package deal, but would not be drawn on whether he accepted the link. “I’m going to be fighting hard for these benefits for Britain in the next seven days … they will make a real difference. If I can do anything to address the cost of living crisis, I should be doing it.”

He has previously said the food and drink deal, which will ease Brexit red tape, will add 0.4% to British GDP.

The prime minister also said David Cameron had been wrong to argue that Britain’s problems had “nothing to do with Brexit”, adding there would be “long nights ahead” to negotiate a reset with the EU before the summit.

Cameron, the prime minister who lost the 2016 Brexit referendum, told Bloomberg News that Burnham should not seek to bring Britain back into the EU, arguing that the UK’s problems had nothing to do with its exit from the EU.

Asked about those remarks, Burnham said: “I think he is wrong to say that the low growth that we’ve had over the last decade has, quote, ‘nothing to do with Brexit’. I would say the evidence says otherwise.

“It feels like his intervention is more about unity in the Conservative party than it is about fighting for the British interests.”

Burnham has recently said he is open to rejoining the single market, customs union or to “go all the way” by rejoining the EU. He said a deeper relationship would be the outcome of future talks “and it will be in the outcome of that negotiation that then we will take a decision as a cabinet, on what, if anything, comes next”.

Earlier on Thursday, the EU foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said she wanted to see Britain rejoin the EU, but warned that negotiations would not be easy after the “trauma” of the Brexit years.

She said: “I would very much like to see Britain back in Europe, but, of course, we also have in the European Union , a lot of, I would say, trauma from Britain leaving, so the negotiations will not be that easy.”

Burnham is expected to make the EU reset the centrepiece of his white-tie speech at the lord mayor’s banquet on Monday night – though it will range widely across foreign policy challenges.

No 10 sources said the speech would be focused on the upcoming Brussels summit – and look ahead to the next stage in 2027 – rather than outline what a more permanent close relationship might look like.

Officials at the UK-EU summit will also discuss the agenda for the next round of the reset, expected to focus on a joint migration pact.

It could also target collaboration on law enforcement and borders, visas for touring artists, and mutual recognition of qualifications.

Ministry of Justice officials are also trying to water down an EU ultimatum on halting the deportation of foreign national offenders. “This is the classic wheeze that the EU always pulls at the last minute of negotiations,” one Whitehall source said.

The next week is expected to be fraught with last-minute negotiations. Key will be access to Made in Europe, which has the potential to lock British firms out of continental supply chains and public contracts if no deal is done.

Negotiations could be challenging despite the lure of the UK making a potential concession on tuition fees in exchange for inclusion in the Made in Europe legislation .

The EU has long said there cannot be a deal on Made in Europe at the summit, because it has yet to finalise its own position.

The joint communique for 2027 is expected to call for strengthening efforts between the UK and the most exposed member states to the small boats crisis in the Channel.

This will centre on both the EU’s Channel action plan, already in place since June this year, and a possible framework for a wider bespoke EU-UK migration plan.

The UK is believed to be pushing for access to the Eurodac database, which carries the fingerprints of asylum seekers, as well as to the Schengen Information System (SIS), which records details on fugitives, missing people and stolen goods.

The UK was the third biggest user of SIS before it lost access through Brexit.

items.title: The Guardian view on venture capitalism: investor profits are no industrial strategy | Editorial

items.content:
Higher returns for backers do not guarantee national prosperity. Public investment should develop domestic capabilities and meet urgent social needs

Britain keeps selling its most valuable companies. The Financial Times calculates that 300 went to foreign buyers, mostly American, over the past decade. What if innovation were scaled up to serve social needs here rather than US investors’ profits? That is the provocation issued by the thinktank Common Wealth in a paper titled We Aren’t the Champions, which takes aim at the UK’s venture capital (VC) industry.

The authors say that as long as the UK is subordinated to US cash, getting startups to a heavyweight size will be a sisyphean task. Britain’s tech pioneers are often sold before they become giants. DeepMind, founded in London in 2010, went to Google just four years later. Britain’s venture capitalists might argue that they are in it for themselves, not for building up British tech.

Higher returns for backers do not guarantee national prosperity. Public investment should develop domestic capabilities and meet urgent social needs

B ritain keeps selling its most valuable companies. The Financial Times calculates that 300 went to foreign buyers, mostly American, over the past decade. What if innovation were scaled up to serve social needs here rather than US investors’ profits? That is the provocation issued by the thinktank Common Wealth in a paper titled We Aren’t the Champions, which takes aim at the UK’s venture capital (VC) industry.

The authors say that as long as the UK is subordinated to US cash, getting startups to a heavyweight size will be a sisyphean task . Britain’s tech pioneers are often sold before they become giants. DeepMind, founded in London in 2010, went to Google just four years later. Britain’s venture capitalists might argue that they are in it for themselves, not for building up British tech.

The conventional wisdom is that if startups are struggling to grow, the problem must be that they lack capital. That is why Rachel Reeves, as chancellor, wanted pension funds to invest in UK assets. But the paper says that this risks making things worse. Putting cash into startups risks inflating eventual sale prices without securing British ownership or control.

The London School of Economics’ Nils Peters and David Kampmann expose a circular logic. The UK lacks tech giants that can acquire successful startups, but selling those startups overseas helps perpetuate that problem. The authors say US and European incumbents won big from the exit of the 38 biggest UK VC-backed tech firms between 2010 and 2023, including businesses at the forefront of AI, fintech and biotechnology.

Selling British technology companies abroad can enrich investors while thwarting ambitions to build domestic champions. The social costs also matter. A system geared towards maximising capital gains favours businesses that promise lucrative exits. The paper argues that this has encouraged surveillance technologies, from wearables to AI chatbots, and exploitative gig platforms , concentrating wealth among a few rather than delivering social benefits.

Gordon Brown is right: Britain should retain ownership of its innovations. But there is a difference between financial returns and industrial development – and improving the former doesn’t necessarily deliver the latter. Although industrial policy has returned rhetorically in the west, this has not translated into meaningful policy. The Common Wealth paper suggests that is a mistake and argues for democratic control over innovation, with investment directed towards social purposes.

The paper’s preferred capitalism is one that is historically associated with the global south: curbing extractive intermediaries, limiting foreign capital and building domestic capacity. India’s publicly funded space programme and Ethiopia’s state-owned airline show how sustained public investment can support homegrown capabilities rather than hastily readying businesses for sale.

Most daringly, Brazil linked universal healthcare for 215 million people to industrial policy, using public purchasing, laboratories and technology transfer. The payoff came during the pandemic: by August 2021, almost three-quarters of Covid vaccine doses administered had been produced at home. Brazil shows that a state can finance, research and produce a universal healthcare system that creates employment and productive capacity. It is surely a powerful idea that providing for people could be a way of sustaining output. Making the fulfilment of social needs a motor of economic development would give Labour a purpose beyond managing scarcity.

items.title: Jensen Huang was a busted flush at Nvidia – he had to go | Nils Pratley

items.content:
CEO was viewed as ‘irreplaceable’, but recklessness of affair with a woman regarded by US officials as a Chinese spy made him a political liability

Half the tech world made up its mind before the facts could be assessed properly. Jensen Huang was “irreplaceable”, said the chorus at the start of this week. Nvidia would melt without the co-founder’s brilliance, apparently. The chipmaker’s board had to find a way to save its genius for the sake of corporate America and the entire AI universe.

It was always nonsense because, after the passage of only a few days since his confession of infidelity, Huang looked less like a towering corporate titan and more like a political liability.

items.lbText:
CEO was viewed as ‘irreplaceable’, but recklessness of affair with a woman regarded by US officials as a Chinese spy made him a political liability

H alf the tech world made up its mind before the facts could be assessed properly. Jensen Huang was “irreplaceable”, said the chorus at the start of this week. Nvidia would melt without the co-founder’s brilliance, apparently. The chipmaker’s board had to find a way to save its genius for the sake of corporate America and the entire AI universe.

It was always nonsense because, after the passage of only a few days since his confession of infidelity, Huang looked less like a towering corporate titan and more like a political liability.

An extramarital affair is not usually a resigning matter in itself – saintliness is not an absolute requirement of the job. But the circumstances here were different. A relationship with the Chinese boss of a Singapore-based firm suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips into China? That displayed recklessness on top of mere unfaithfulness.

Did he know the Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang (no relation), was regarded as a Chinese spy by US officials? It hardly matters. In the ultra-political world of in-demand AI computer chips, there were enough reasons for him to be careful in the extreme. The conflict of interest, and the risk of landing Nvidia in a quagmire of national security inquiries in Washington, would have been obvious.

Reports of a second affair with a senior Nvidia employee compounded matters – US companies tend to be sensitive about such relationships. But the company’s directors might also have wondered what else could be revealed in coming weeks. Rule number one in these situations is to get all the bad news out on day one.

The kneejerk reaction to Jensen Huang’s resignation was 13% off the share price. That was understandable – some investors truly believed the “irreplaceable” thesis. However, sitting in Nvidia’s boardroom, the job was not to worry about the initial stock market response but about what was best for the business. For multiple reasons, it was time to “rip off the Band-Aid and take Nvidia into its next chapter”, as Dan Ives, a senior tech analyst, put it.

First, the congressional investigations will happen anyway. Democratic senators have asked administration officials to preserve all documents and communications related to the sale of Nvidia’s advanced AI chips to China. At heart, that issue is wider than Nvidia – it’s about whether US officials have themselves jeopardised the country’s lead over China in AI. But, one way or another, the company’s activities, and ties to the Trump administration , will come under scrutiny like never before. Nvidia is better placed to defend itself without Huang in the top job.

Second, his personal lobbying clout on export policy had evaporated. After this week’s revelations, he had no credibility as an advocate of looser restrictions. The political demand will be entirely in the other direction – for loopholes to be closed.

Third, there is the issue Nvidia’s underpowered board has dodged for too long: over-reliance on one individual. Never mind the risk of scandal, there is always a danger in concentrating too much day-to-day power in the hands of one individual. Nobody doubts Huang’s commercial talents, but even “godfathers of AI” in leather jackets don’t go on forever. Better to have a setup that can cope with change at the top.

Colette Kress, the chief financial officer who will stand in as chief executive, is well regarded on Wall Street. Nvidia will not be short of outside applicants on a permanent basis. And the board has heard the governance criticism that a multitrillion-dollar company ought to have an independent chair: Harvey Jones, a former chief executive at semiconductor company Synopsys and a member of the current crew of directors, has got the gig. Then comes the task of creating some proper governance checks and balances, which may require fresh faces among the independent directors.

Within a couple of hours, the fall in the share price had narrowed to 5% as investors remembered that Nvidia still has the best, and most in-demand, graphics processing units in the world and that many pioneering companies have prospered after the exit of an “irreplaceable” chief executive.

Nobody pretends the management job will be easy. Nvidia will be different, not least because the political winds in the US have shifted. But there was no point trying to cling to a chief executive, however successful, who had made himself a busted flush. Huang had to go.

items.lbText:
Technical expertise and an ability to engage gave the chipmaker’s co-founder, who has now resigned, the edge with customers and investors

Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO after alleged affairs

Jensen Huang wasn’t always in his trademark leather jacket. When the multibillionaire, now former Nvidia chief executive was a teenager in the US, his first job was waiting tables and washing dishes at a branch of Denny’s.

“It teaches you humility, it teaches you hard work, it teaches you hospitality,” he said in 2023 of his time at the diner chain.

Decades later, having become one of the richest people on the planet, Huang put on a Denny’s apron in tribute to his former employer at an Nvidia event in 2025.

By this point Huang had become a rockstar of the artificial intelligence boom – befitting his signature item of clothing – feted around the world by investors, fellow tech executives and politicians.

The company that Huang co-founded makes the computer chips that are integral to the development and operation of AI systems such as ChatGPT.

Demand for Nvidia’s products has surged as hundreds of billions of dollars have been poured into a technology that, according to its many promotors, will transform the global economy. The crude analogy is that Huang and Nvidia have become the main purveyors of shovels in the AI gold rush.

In technical jargon, its AI chips are known as graphics processor units (GPUs), which were originally designed to handle the graphics for video games. But it turned out that a GPU’s ability to carry out masses of technical calculations simultaneously and quickly is very handy for developing and operating AI systems, which have a voracious appetite for data crunching.

Nvidia is also very good at creating networks of its chips, which produces the computing power artificial intelligence needs, and provides the CUDA software that helps the company’s GPUs perform so well for AI customers.

Jen-Hsun Huang, 63, was born in Taiwan to a chemical engineer father and a schoolteacher mother. Decades later, the island would become the centre of chip manufacturing and the foundry for Nvidia’s highly advanced chips.

But his life was largely lived outside Taiwan. After a spell living in Thailand, Huang moved to the US when he was 10 – he is a joint citizen of Taiwan and the US – and has said he is “always an immigrant”.

Accidentally enrolled by his uncle into a juvenile reform school in Kentucky, he anglicised his name and showed educational flair. Huang went to high school in Oregon and in 1984 he graduated with a degree in electrical engineering from Oregon State University, where he met his future wife, Lori, with whom he had a son and a daughter, both now Nvidia employees.

He then completed a master’s degree in the same subject at Stanford University – in the heart of Silicon Valley – in 1992. A year later he founded Nvidia with fellow engineers Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, during a meeting in a booth at Denny’s. The name is a riff on the Latin term for envy, invidia , an emotion that the company wanted its rivals to feel.

Huang’s technical expertise also gave him an edge with customers and investors, according to The Nvidia Way, a biography of the company and its co-founder by Tae Kim.

The book quotes Tench Coxe, an Nvidia board member and early investor, who said Huang stood out.

“When you meet Jensen Huang, even with dozens of other graphics companies, you realise this is a guy you want to do business with,” said Tench. “What made him great is he is an engineer and he is a computer scientist.”

Nvidia started out making graphics chips for personal computers. It released what is widely regarded as the world’s first GPU, the GeForce 256, in 1999 and as the technology became more and more powerful academic researchers realised it could accelerate AI development. Nvidia GPUs were used to create AlexNet, the neural network developed by Alex Krizhevsky, the OpenAI-co-founder Ilya Sutskever and the Nobel prize winner Geoffrey Hinton at the University of Toronto in 2012 – and a key moment in the history of modern AI.

Six months after the launch of ChatGPT, Nvidia’s valuation reached $1tn (£756bn) in May 2023 and kept growing, hitting $5tn on October last year – the first ever company to reach such a milestone . However, it has fallen to about $4tn this week after allegations that Huang had conducted affairs with a Chinese spy and an Nvidia executive, leading to his resignation on Thursday.

Huang’s 3.6% stake in Nvidia has given him considerable wealth. His fortune is valued at $145bn, according to Bloomberg, the 13th highest in the world.

The importance of Nvidia’s products to the AI revolution have made Huang rich, powerful and famous. He is often seen at tech conferences or in the presence of global leaders, including Donald Trump with whom he has developed a rapport. Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, another mighty Silicon Valley founder, has described Huang as “Taylor Swift, but for tech”.

One UK tech industry insider who has met Huang at various tech and government events describes the Nvidia CEO as having an “ability to engage” that marked him out from other executives in his peer group.

“He’s like a good politician,” said the source. “I think the sector has lost one of its best communicators.”

The source added that Huang had no problem getting access to the upper echelons of governments. “Everyone wanted to meet him.”

However, Huang’s undoubted drive and charisma had a flipside, according to Stephen Witt, a journalist who interviewed the executive as part of his award-winning book about Huang and his company, The Thinking Games. In his final chat with a “visibly exhausted” Huang in 2024, Witt describes the interviewee’s voice “crescendoing with anger” as he mulls a question about what new jobs will be created by AI.…

items.lbText:
Battery maker CATL aims to have 2,000 swapping stations in China by the end of 2027 and to bring the tech to Europe

E very day, Wang Bing drives his big electric lorry to send about five tonnes of goods between the cities of Haikou and Dongfang on Hainan, a tropical island in southern China . A round trip covers about 500 kilometres (310 miles). But refuelling is not something Wang worries about.

“When my battery runs low, I just drive my truck into a battery-swapping station to get a fully charged one,” says the 53-year-old, who shares the journey with a colleague in eight-hour shifts.

Wang has been a lorry driver for nearly three decades. In the first two of those, he drove conventional lorries fuelled by diesel. About five years ago, he began driving an electric model after the logistics company he worked for upgraded its fleet. In July this year, his old e-truck, which used conventional plug-in charging, was replaced by one with a swappable battery.

In the past, Wang had to spend an hour and half charging his battery each time, but with his new truck, it takes just five minutes or so to have a drained battery removed and a fresh one replaced. “I am very happy,” he says.

Battery swapping is not new in China, where more than 400,000 e-trucks (or over 90% of the global total ) were sold last year. The Chinese carmaker Nio commercialised the technology nearly a decade ago for smaller electric vehicles (EVs). But in 2023, the Chinese battery behemoth CATL launched a battery-swapping system for electric lorries through a subsidiary brand called Qiji Energy.

To Wang, the biggest advantage of the technology is the time it saves. “It is much, much faster,” he says. “I don’t even need to leave my truck when the battery is being swapped.”

This swiftness builds on the cost advantage e-trucks already have over their fossil-fuelled peers when it comes to refuelling.

“Electricity is cheaper than oil,” Wang says. The per-kilometre fuelling cost for an e-truck works out about 1.1 yuan (12p) in Hainan, he says, significantly lower than that for a diesel truck, which exceeds 2 yuan (22p) a kilometre. “That means my e-truck can save more than 20,000 yuan (£2,200) per month,” Wang says.

When a truck approaches a battery-swapping station, the station’s cameras automatically identify the type of battery it uses by checking its number plate. “All the driver needs to do is to drive the truck into a designated area, and the battery will be swapped completely automatically,” says Wei Jiuchun, 46, a test driver at a Qiji Energy battery-swapping station in Suzhou, east China. Wei’s job is to help the station test its system for different models of heavy trucks and under different weather conditions.

It is not just time and fuel costs the technology saves but, in China, the initial lump sum a buyer has to put down to get an e-truck, says Mao Shiyue, a Beijing-based researcher at the International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT).

The upfront purchase price for an e-truck is significantly higher than for a comparable diesel model, a major obstacle for those vehicles’ wider adoption in many parts of the world. In China, a customer opting for battery swapping typically buys an e-truck without a battery, and then rents the battery from a service provider. As the cost of a battery is about 40% of an e-truck’s price, the business model can make e-trucks a lot more affordable, Mao says.

The technology can also help minimise the pressure EV charging brings to the power grid, according to Mao, because swapping stations have more flexibility to spread out the charging time for the depleted batteries.

“If the grid sees a spike in electricity demand during peak hours, those stations can even act as an energy-storage station by returning the electricity stored in their batteries back to the grid to ease the strain,” he says.

CATL, the world’s biggest battery manufacturer, is a key player in promoting battery swapping for heavy trucks in China. The company’s support for the technology is critical for its large-scale rollout, says Phate Zhang, the founder of CnEVPost, a Shanghai-based outlet focusing on EVs.

CATL plans to put 900 battery-swapping stations into operation across China by the end of this year, expanding its current network twice more. By the end of 2027, it wants the number to reach 2,000.

The company has also teamed up with the London-based renewable energy supplier Octopus to bring the technology to Europe. It intends to open its first group of battery-swapping “mega hubs” in the UK next year, and a network of more than 30 hubs in Europe by 2035.

In China, battery-swapping is still a minority charging method for its rapidly growing e-truck fleet. In 2024, about one-third of the zero-emission trucks in the country featured this technology, while the rest largely had conventional plug-in charging, according to the latest available figures .

One downside is that drivers often need to stick to a particular service provider that caters to the specific type of swappable batteries their e-trucks use.

“For example, some batteries are swapped from the chassis, while others are swapped from the top of the truck,” says Xue Lulu, a senior associate at World Resources Institute China. “Even under the same technological route, batteries made by different companies often have different specifications.” This means drivers cannot drop into any random swapping station to get their trucks replenished, which could restrict the journeys they can make, she says.

Plus, battery swapping doesn’t necessarily mean drivers will save time, Xue says. During her field research in China, she found some lorry drivers would wait outside battery-swapping stations for one to two hours before going in because they wanted to avoid using the service during peak hours, to save money. “Logistics firms are extremely sensitive to costs,” she says.…

items.lbText:
Despite John Healey’s defiance, the economy faces threats from a tech slowdown and energy bills this winter

AI helps UK economy grow at fastest pace for more than two years

The forecasters were clear when John Healey became chancellor in July: Britain’s resilience to the war in the Middle East would not last. The global economic headwinds were too strong, inflation was beginning to rise and growth would slow to a trickle.

Four months into the job, the economy is continuing to defy expectations after growing by 0.7% in the third quarter – the fastest expansion in two and a half years. It puts the UK on course to be the second-fastest growing G7 economy this year.

On his first day in Downing Street the memo from the Treasury showed the most optimistic City analyst expected 0.3% quarterly growth. Most had pencilled in a figure close to zero. Some were warning that the UK could edge towards a recession.

Despite the gloomy outlook households have continued to spend and business investment has powered ahead, driven by the rollout of AI.

Underneath the bonnet, growth is being spearheaded by IT and professional services – together contributing about half of the rise in activity. As the central sectors in the AI boom, that is hardly surprising – with analysts at ING suggesting the strength in IT was “very clearly a datacentre story” thanks to the UK’s status as a leading destination in Europe for investment.

Overall, Deutsche Bank estimates that AI-related spending has added about 0.3% to 0.4% to GDP growth this year. It is clear to see why Healey is keen to build on the groundwork laid by his immediate predecessor, Rachel Reeves, to harness AI amid government efforts to court global business investment.

Meanwhile, household consumption is up by 1.6% so far this year – helped by spending over the warm summer months even as consumers faced a living standards squeeze because the Iran war fuelled a surge in petrol and diesel prices.

However, the fear is that the UK’s initial resilience to the global economic storm emanating from the Middle East will soon fizzle out.

Both of Britain’s recent growth engines face a tougher period ahead.

After the US midterm elections and revelations at the chipmaker Nvidia , the outlook for the AI investment boom is less certain. Financial markets have been rocked in recent weeks amid fears that a bubble in AI stocks could be about to burst . A slowdown in technology investment could hit the UK. Still, the hope is that swelling demand for AI will not evaporate overnight.

For households, however, a tough winter lies ahead. Energy bills are poised to increase by about a quarter in January, with the average annual household gas and electricity bill expected to climb to more than £2,000. Analysts say it is hard to see how consumer spending would not come under greater pressure in the new year.

In the latest data there were some early warning signs: retail sales and consumer discretionary spending fell in September. Real wage growth is cooling and the headline inflation rate is on track to reach a fresh peak of close to 5% next year.

With growth proving resilient, the Bank of England will feel emboldened to raise interest rates to combat imported inflation. City investors expect at least two more quarter-point increases to 4.5% before the end of next year. That will hit the brakes on the economy and add to the cost of living squeeze.

At last month’s budget Healey struck a defiant tone by arguing that the UK could continue to defy forecasters expectations. That task, however, is becoming increasingly tough.

items.lbText:
Pump prices stay stubbornly high as leading bank official warns energy costs are likely to remain ‘elevated’

The price of diesel on UK forecourts remains stubbornly close to October’s record high of £2 despite a sharp fall in oil prices.

A litre costs an average of 197p, according to the AA, which described the situation as “dismal”. By contrast, petrol has fallen 6p to 168p from the peak of 174.7p in early October. That was the highest level since August 2022.

High fuel prices are putting huge financial strain on households and businesses and Christopher Waller, a US Federal Reserve governor, told a conference in London this week that energy prices could remain “elevated”.

He said a rise in tanker traffic through the strait of Hormuz came at a price: “The insurance now needed for ships making this passage, and the ship-to-ship transfer of oil necessary to guard against Iranian attacks, are reportedly boosting oil prices by $20 to $30 a barrel.”

Diesel production is also being affected by limited refining capacity and other constraints, Waller said, adding: “As a consequence, elevated prices for diesel in the United States are not expected to moderate as readily as crude oil prices would in a more peaceful Middle East.”

In the UK, the AA said that another 10p reduction could be on the cards for petrol because wholesale costs were falling. The wholesale cost of unleaded fell from 77p a litre to 68p in the second half of October, and now sits below 62p.

As a rule of thumb, each 5p reduction at the pump knocks £2.75 off the cost of filling a typical car’s 55-litre tank.

Luke Bosdet, the AA’s spokesperson on pump prices, said it was “hit and miss” but already possible to find petrol below 160p in certain areas, based on the government’s fuel finder data.

“London and the south-east stand out for not showing any fuel stations with the bargain petrol prices of northern England, Wales and even Scotland,” he said. “Some forecourts are still charging close to the peak prices of early October and, given how much wholesale costs have fallen since the middle of last month, that is unforgivable.”

The average diesel price is down only 2p a litre, from the all-time record of £2. With the wholesale cost down around 4p a litre since mid-October a further small reduction at the pump was possible, Bosdet said.

items.lbText:
Kemi Badenoch attacked reforms but is not being clear about how party would meet costs, Torsten Bell claims

Kemi Badenoch’s Conservatives would have to raise the state pension age above 70 to meet the cost of keeping the triple lock, Treasury minister Torsten Bell has claimed.

Labour has announced reforms to the triple-lock promise to come into force in the next parliament – with the initial proceeds earmarked for Andy Burnham’s national care service.

The Conservatives have attacked the move, and insisted they would stick with the triple lock, which increases the state pension each year in line with the largest of inflation, 2.5% or earnings growth.

However, Bell argued that with the costs of an unreformed triple lock increasing over time – to £50bn by 2050, according to government estimates – a Tory government would end up repeating the approach they took in the 2010s and speeding up planned increases to the state pension age.

“If you don’t want to have an adjustment to the triple lock, then you will need to do other things to make the state pension remotely sustainable,” he said. “We don’t need to guess what they would do because they’ve literally just done it, which is they repeatedly and at very short notice accelerated the increases in the state pension age.

“They did that in the in 2011 and in 2014. Some people had as little as five years’ notice.”

In 2013, the then chancellor, George Osborne, described increasing the pension age as, “one of the less controversial things we have done,” which had nevertheless delivered “absolutely enormous savings”.

The state pension age, now under review, is already expected to increase to 68 between 2044 and 2046; but Bell claimed the Conservatives would end up going further.

“All I’m saying is, Conservatives do raise the state pension age aggressively, and they have,” he said. “And even though they know that the triple lock should change, they are opposing it – and the consequence of that is they would end up making people wait into their 70s.”

The triple lock had previously been seen as too politically risky to reform, particularly in the light of the backlash against Labour’s plan to remove the winter fuel allowance from the vast majority of pensioners – which was subsequently abandoned .

But Bell said the public would prefer Burnham’s willingness to make an argument to what he claimed was the Conservatives’ failure to be honest.

“I think this is a bigger problem for Kemi Badenoch than she thinks. She thinks that her brand is principled, know what you think, tell it straight. And on this, she has done the opposite – we know that she knows it needs to change,” he said.

He cited the Conservative leader’s own suggestion, as recently as last year, that the triple lock should be means tested , and former Conservative chancellor Jeremy Hunt’s claim that the policy was an “anchor drag” on the public finances.

“The triple lock kind of is the final nail in the coffin of the idea that there’s anything fiscally responsible about modern Conservatism,” Bell said.

Under Labour’s planned reforms , the state pension will rise each year by the highest of inflation, or 2.5%. It will only rise in line with earnings growth if its value has slipped behind recent wage growth.

Bell, the MP for Swansea West since 2024, was previously director of the Resolution Foundation thinktank. He retained his role as pensions minister – working between the Treasury and the Department for Work and Pensions – when Burnham came to power in July.

He said the prime minister’s 10-year plan, which may now be delayed until the new year, will include a promise of a better deal for future pensioners. “It’s just really important to be able to say to people, ‘the comfortable retirement that your parents had: we’re going to make sure that today’s private sector workers have got those’,” he added.
